sentences.text: The only known species of the genus Panguraptor is Panguraptor lufengensis, a partial articulated skeleton of a subadult individual estimated to have been approximately 2 meters long in life.
Conserved teeth in the dentary and maxilla were slightly recurved but lacked serrations, suggesting a specific dietary niche within its ecosystem.
The hand had four digits, with the first and second metacarpals being the widest, while the first toe possessed a flattened, recurved claw that was the largest found in the holotype.
Its vertebral column featured ten cervical vertebrae and thirteen sacral vertebrae, and the foot included a rudimentary fifth metatarsal bone.
The exposed nasal portions of Panguraptor are wide and smooth, lacking a sagittal crest found in some other basal theropods.
The first digit possessed a flattened and recurved claw, which is the largest claw in the holotype, a feature that distinguishes it from many contemporaries.
Panguraptor is distinguished from other coelophysids by a diagonal ridge on the maxilla, an elliptical fenestra, and a distal tarsal IV with a hooked corner.
The genus was described in 2014 by You Hai-Lu and colleagues, formally introducing this new predator to scientific record.
The holotype specimen was recovered on October 12, 2007, from the Lufeng Formation in Yunnan Province, specifically on a hillside behind Xiaolishu Village in Lufeng County, China.

Because of weathering, the partially exposed skeleton was glued and plastered on site over two days before being shipped to a museum, where the fossil catalogued as LFGT-0103 was formally described in 2014 as the type specimen of Panguraptor lufengensis.

The skull is quite short and nearly complete, though the premaxilla, rostral margin of the maxilla, and nasals are partially missing or destroyed, while the preserved teeth are slightly recurved but unserrated.
The vertebral column possessed ten cervical vertebrae and thirteen sacral vertebrae, the foot included a rudimentary fifth metatarsal bone, and the second and third metatarsals were the longest.
Cladistic analysis places Panguraptor within Coelophysoidea and specifically within the family Coelophysidae, grouping it with Coelophysis, Megapnosaurus, and Camposaurus.
Panguraptor is considered the first coelophysoid known from Asia and represents the first good material of a coelophysid found in China or even Asia.
A 2026 analysis recovered Panguraptor as a basal member of the superfamily Coelophysoidea, and it is more closely related to Coelophysis bauri than to "Syntarsus" kayentakatae.
Panguraptor lived during the Early Jurassic, approximately 199.3 million years ago, specifically during the Hettangian stage, between 201.4 and 199.5 million years ago.
The sediments containing Panguraptor are dated to the late Sinemurian to possibly Toarcian stages, indicating a slightly later or overlapping temporal range in some interpretations.

Other small coelophysid specimens from the Lufeng Formation, such as FMNH CUP 2089 and FMNH CUP 2090, may belong to Panguraptor but have been provisionally named "Megapnosaurus" kayentakatae pending further analysis.
